title: Sequence of tenses

objectives.can: Explain why a subordinate subjunctive stands in the tense it does.

explanation.summary: The tense of a subordinate subjunctive depends on the tense of the main verb and on whether the subordinate action is the same time or later, or earlier. A present main verb is followed by a present or perfect subjunctive, and a past main verb by an imperfect or pluperfect. This is the sequence of tenses, and it explains the form of nearly every subjunctive clause you have met.

sections.heading: The subjunctive's tense is relative
body: The tense of an indicative verb places the action in time. The tense of a subjunctive in a subordinate clause does something else: it shows how the subordinate action stands to the main verb. That is why an imperfect subjunctive in Latin is not simply 'past', and why the present subjunctive of a purpose clause is not always translated with a present.

Compare John 17:15, *Non rogo ut tollas eos de mundo, sed ut serves eos a malo*, with Luke 8:31, *Et rogabant illum ne imperaret illis*. Both clauses are indirect commands. The first has present subjunctives (*tollas*, *serves*) because the main verb *rogo* is present. The second has an imperfect (*imperaret*) because the main verb *rogabant* is past.

sections.heading: Primary and secondary main verbs
body: Grammarians divide main verbs into two groups. Primary tenses are the present, the future, the future perfect, the perfect meaning 'has done', and the imperative (a command looks ahead). Secondary tenses are the imperfect, the pluperfect and the perfect when it means a simple past event. After a primary main verb the subjunctive stands in the present or the perfect. After a secondary main verb it stands in the imperfect or the pluperfect.

Within each group the choice depends on time. A present (after primary) or an imperfect (after secondary) subjunctive shows an action at the same time as the main verb or after it. A perfect (after primary) or a pluperfect (after secondary) shows an action that happened before the main verb.

sections.heading: Seeing the rule in indirect questions
body: Indirect questions show the time relation most clearly. In John 3:8 *nescis unde veniat aut quo vadat*, 'you do not know where it comes from or where it goes', the main verb *nescis* is present and the clauses are present subjunctive, the same time as the not-knowing. In John 13:12 *Scitis quid fecerim vobis?* the main verb is present, but the action asked about is earlier, so the subjunctive is perfect: 'do you know what I have done to you?'.

After a past main verb the same relation appears in the secondary tenses. Luke 1:29 says Mary *cogitabat qualis esset ista salutatio*: she was wondering what sort of greeting this was. Both verbs are imperfect, and the subordinate action was at the same time as the main one. In Mark 15:44 Pilate *mirabatur si jam obiisset*, 'wondered whether he had already died'. The pluperfect *obiisset* places the death before the wondering.
In Matthew 24:42 *nescitis qua hora Dominus vester venturus sit* the present *sit* with the future participle *venturus* looks ahead: the coming is later than the not-knowing.

sections.heading: The perfect main verb has two faces
body: A perfect tense can mean 'has done' (a past act that still matters) or just 'did' (a past event told as a story). In the first sense Latin treats it as primary, in the second as secondary. John 20:31 has *Hæc autem scripta sunt ut credatis*: the writing is complete, but it is still there for the reader, so the present *credatis* follows. Matthew 1:22 has *Hoc autem totum factum est, ut adimpleretur quod dictum est*: the events belong to the past story, so the imperfect *adimpleretur* follows.

The same applies to John 3:17, *Non enim misit Deus Filium suum in mundum, ut judicet mundum, sed ut salvetur mundus*, where the sending is viewed as an act with lasting effect, so the present subjunctives follow. Only the sense of the sentence shows which face the perfect has, and sometimes both are possible.

sections.heading: Where the Vulgate departs from the rule
body: A Latin translation does not always follow the classical rule. In Luke 8:47 the woman *indicavit* (a simple past) why she touched him, and the Vulgate writes *ob quam causam tetigerit eum* and *quemadmodum confestim sanata sit* with perfect subjunctives. Classical writers would usually put pluperfects after a past main verb, so this is looser. The clauses are read as indirect questions, and the Vulgate's perfect subjunctive after a past main verb is not an error to correct.

Result clauses are also less strict. In 1 Thessalonians 1:8 the main verb is the perfect *profecta est*, and the result clause is *ita ut non sit nobis necesse quidquam loqui*, with a present subjunctive: the result still holds. In Mark 4:37 the waves *mittebat in navim, ita ut impleretur navis*: the main verb is an imperfect and the result clause is imperfect too, as the rule predicts. A result clause can follow the time of the result as the writer sees it, not only the tense of the main verb.
So treat the rule as a strong tendency. If a verse does not follow it, ask what the writer meant by the tense, and do not alter the text.

misunderstandings: Reading an imperfect subjunctive as 'would' or as a pure past tense. It often only marks a clause whose main verb is past, and in a purpose clause it looks forward from that past moment.
Reading a present subjunctive as a present tense in English. In a purpose clause after a primary main verb it points forward.
Treating every perfect main verb as secondary. A perfect meaning 'has done' (John 20:31) takes primary sequence.
Using the sequence of tenses to decide what kind of clause it is. The sequence tells you the tense of the verb, not whether the clause is purpose, result or question.

deeper.heading: Why the rule exists
body: Latin speakers felt the subordinate clause as part of the point of view of the main verb. When the main verb looked back from the present, the subordinate clause shared that point of view. When it was told as a past story, the clause was seen from a past moment. The rule is a way of keeping the clauses at one point of view, and the Vulgate is sometimes looser about it.

reading.why: A short narrative where the sequence is easy to follow: past main verbs with imperfect subjunctives (*cum esset desponsata*, *antequam convenirent*, *ut adimpleretur*), and the angel's speech in the present. Find the main verb of each clause first, then ask what the tense of the subjunctive tells you.
